FOREWORD 


This Indian Standard (Part 34) (First Revision) was adopted by the Bureau of Indian Standards, after the draft 
finalized by the Conductors and Accessories for Overhead Lines Sectional Committee had been approved by the 
Electrotechnical Division Council. 


This standard was originally published in 1972. This revision has been brought out to bring the standard in the 
latest style and format of the Indian Standards. 


The definitions contained in this standard have been drawn up with the object of striking a correct balance between 
absolute precision and simplicity. The principal object of the standard is to provide definitions which are 
sufficiently clear so that each term is understood with the same meaning by all the users and it does not, therefore, 
constitute a treatise on cinematographic terminology. Definitions are not sufficiently precise, do not include all 
cases, do not take account of certain exception or are not identical with those which may be found in other 
publications designed with other objects and for other readers, such imperfections, which will be eliminated as far 
as possible in later editions, arc inevitable and should be accepted in the interest of simplicity and clarity. 


The composition of the Committee responsible for formulation of this standard is given in Annex A. 


For the purpose of deciding whether a particular requirement of this standard is complied with the final value, 
observed or calculated expressing the result of a test or analysis shall be rounded off in accordance with 
IS 2 : 2022 ‘Rules for rounding of numerical values (second revision)’. The number of significant places retained 
in the rounded off value should be the same as that of the specified value in this standard. 


IS 1885 (Part 34) : 2023 


Indian Standard 
ELECTROTECHNICAL VOCABULARY 
PART 34 CINEMATOGRAPHY 


( First Revision ) 


1 SCOPE 


This standard (Part 34) covers terms used in the field 
of cinematography. 


2 TERMINOLOGY 


2.1 Absolute Film — Experimental film in/which 
the real objects are not the medium of the narration. 


2.2 Achromatic Leas — A combination of a 
concave lens of flint glass and a convex lens of 
crown glass to remove or reduce chromatic 
aberration. 


2.3 Acuity Meter — Apparatus for measuring the 
degree of acuity. 


2.4 Added Scenes — Made to ensure that the filmed 
story is well rounded, usually after the takings 
according to the script. 


2.5 Aging — The total effect of deterioration to a 
film due to wear and/or storage. 


2.6 Air Fog — Phenomenon in the processed film 
due to air present one of the baths. 


2.7 All Bottom Sound — Sound in which low 
frequencies predominate. 


2.8 All Top Sound — Sound in which high 
frequencies predominate. 


2.9 Ambit (Contour) — The line forming the 
circumference of an object. 


2.10 Amplifier Box — Portable container for 
amplifiers. 


2.11 Anamorphosing — Term applied in cases 
where anamorph sing of normal pictures occur 
during printing. 


2.12 Anamorphosis — Squeezed picture that by 
means of specially shaped mirrors or lenses may be 
projected as a normal image. 


2.13 Anamorphote Lens — Lens used in large 
screen pictures to project a normal image onto the 
screen from squeezed print, 


2.14 Anamorphotic Picture — Picture taken on the 
principle of anamorphosis. 


2.14.1 Non-Anamorphotic Picture — Picture which 
is not anamorphotic. 


2.15 Angle of Rake (Angle of Projection) — The 
angle which the projector axis makes with the 
horizontal during projection. 


2.16 Angle of Reflection — Angie between a 
reflected ray and the normal (perpendicular) to a 
surface it strikes. 


2.17 Angle Shot — Shot obtained by rolling the 
camera. 


2.18 Animated Cartoon — Film the individual 
images of which are drawn by artists. 


2.19 Animation — The preparing of the cells of a 
cartoon film. 


2.20 Animations — Mechanical devices which 
impart apparent movement to inanimate subjects. 


2.21 Animator — The man who draws the cells of 
an animated cartoon. 


2.22 Apertural Effect — The smallest area in 
which the image of a point source is located. 


2.23 Aperture — An opening that allows passage 
of light through an optical system. 


2.24 Aperture Plate — Plate of metal, 
incorporating the aperture in a projector, printer or 
camera. 


2.25 Apochromatic Lens — Achromatic lens 
corrected for three colours. 


2.26 Apron Tank — Container for processing 
films. 


2.27 Arc Lamp — Lamp with carbon electrodes 
widely used in motion picture projectors. 


2.28 Arc Light — A lighting apparatus containing 
an electric arc as a source of light. 


2.29 Artificial Horizon — Artificial hill against the 
background of which pictures of particular scenes 
are taken. 


2.30 Artificial Light Exposure — Exposure made 
by means of artificial light only. 


IS 1885 (Part 34) : 2023 


2.31 Aspect Ratio — Aspect ratio is the ratio of 
width to height of a projected picture image. 


NOTE — This is the more common usage, although the 
term is also applied, to photographic images and to camera, 
printer and projector apertures. 


2.32 Astigmatism — The effect whereby a parallel 
beam of light with oblique incidence does not give a 
single point at the focus, but two focal lines. 


2.33 Atmospheric Absorption — Absorption of 
energy (sound or light) by air. 


2.34 Audio Mixer — Means in which the output 
signals of two or more sources are mixed. 


2.35 Auditorium Noise — Noise inherent to the 
auditorium or hall itself. 


2.36 Automatic Printing Machine — Machine 
printing sound and pictures in successive 
fully-automatic operations. 


2.37 Automatic Shutter — Device for cutting off 
the lays of light from the film, when the machine 
stops. 


2.38 Avant-Grade film — Film made by artists 
who want to do away with existing trends and try to 
find new ways of expression. 


2.39 Axis of Projection — A straight line from the 
centre of the picture to the center of the projected 
image on the screen. 


2.40 Baby Spot — A lighting equipment containing, 
incandescent lamps with a power of 750 W and 
below and capable of giving a narrow beam of light. 


2.41 Background Film — A picture print 
specifically made for use in project backgrounds. 


2.42 Background Plate (Background Print Film) 
— A background plate (background print film) is a 
picture print made specially for use in projection 
background or similar process work, and is a print 
of a background plate negative. 


2.43 Background Load speaker — Loudspeaker 
for producing the accompanying sound in the studio. 


2.44 Background Music — Music accompanying a 
certain action on the screen and often recorded 
beforehand. 


2.45 Background Projection — Projection of a 
moving or static scenery, used as a background 
during the shooting of a picture. 


2.46 Background Title — Title, the letters of which 
appear on a background other than a uniform area. 


2.47 Backing — Fixed or movable decoration at the 
back of a scene. 


2.48 Back-Light — Projection lamp which 
illuminates the back of the scene. 


2.49 Back-Lighting — Lighting the background 
from a spot which safe-guards against interference 
with the lighting of the rest of the scene. 


2.50 Back Lot — A vast acreage found in 
connection with most studios where exteriors are 
made. 


2.51 Bad Picture — Bad photographic take. 


2.52 Baffle Blanket — Felt or muslin-covered sheet 
hung about a set to absorb sound. 


2.53 Balance Stripe — A magnetic coating or 
coating of another material that is equal in thickness 
to, but may be narrower than the stripe used for 
recording. Primary purpose is to equalize the 
effective thickness of the two edges of the striped 
film in order to obtain uniform winding. The stripe 
is sometimes used for the recording of additional 
sound or control tracks or signal. It is applied along 
the opposite edge of the film. 


2.54 Balancing Blade — The blade of a shutter 
eliminating the flicker on the screen due to the 
shutter movement. 


2.55 Bank of Lights — Rectangular box containing 
a row of incandescent lamps. 


2.56 Barrel Distortion — Distortion of the picture 
in which the sides bulge like a barrel. 


2.57 Barrel Shutter — Shutter of cylindrical form 
in which the obturating blades form part of the 
cylinder surface. 


2.58 Barrier — The thin black track between sound 
track and pictures. 


2.59 Base — Celluloid or acetate component of 
film, on which the emulsion is applied. 


2.59.1 Film Base —The plastic material upon which 
a photographic emulsion is coated, namely, the 
support for the emulsion in the photographic film. 


NOTE — All film, base manufactured for motion picture 
use since 1952 has been safety base. 


2.59.1.1 Safely base — The slow burning film 
support used for motion picture films. 


2.60 Bass Boost — Means to give preferred 
amplification to the lower frequencies. 


2.61 Beam Splitting System — An optical process 
whereby identical multiple copies are obtained 
simultaneously from a single master. 


2.62 Beater Movement — In this method of 
intermittent movement, the film is moved by a series 
of beats, each beat gauged to draw the film down the 
space of one frame. 


2.63 Big Spot — A large rotary lamp. 


2.64 Binocular Matt — A matt placed over the 
camera lens that has an aperture the shape of 
keyhole. 


2.65 Bird's Eye View — A shot taken under a 
certain angle from an elevated spot. 


2.66 Black and White Film — Film containing 
only black and white in the processed film. 


2.67 Lack Drop — A piece of black velvet dropped 
as background for the set to lend a night effect. 


2.68 Bleaching — Bleaching is that part of 
processing which converts a developed silver image 
into a silver salt. 


2.69 Bleeding — Overlapping of colours in colour 
photography. 


2.70 Blimp — Camera cover of soft sound-proof 
material. 


2.71 Blimped-Camera — A camera installed in 
sound-proof casing. 


2.72 Bloop — Low frequency sounds due to poorly 
made blooping-patches. 


2.73 Blooping Notch — A defect in a sound splice. 


2.74 Blow-Up — Term applied in cases where the 
pictures are printed on a film with a larger picture 
format than that of the original film. 


2.75 Blue Glass — A monocle-shaped glass of 
special blue tint used by cinematographers to 
determine colour values of a set, when 
photographing on orthochromatic emulsions. 


2.76 Blue Light — The signal that monitor man 
is-ready and standing by for a take. 


2.77 Blurred Picture — A picture that lacks 
definition to a certain decree. 


2.78 Blurring — The reduction of the apparent 
sharpness of definition of objects in the reproduced 
scene. 


2.79 Blurr Pan — A distorted picture due to a too 
rapidly carried out pan shot. 


IS 1885 (Part 34) : 2023 


2.80 Booster Light — Light used to illuminate 
shadow regions in a scene. 


2.81 Bottom Sprocket — The sprocket which 
transports the film after projection towards the 
take-up spool. 


2.82 Breathing — Film flutter arising out of excess 
heat at the aperture. 


2.83 Brightness — Perfect brightness is that quality 
of the reproduced picture which in its black and 
white parts satisfies the spectator. 


2.84 Buckling — Undesired effect of excessive heat 
on the film. 


2.85 Buzz-Track — Test track with noise 
recordings (see also IS 6561 ). 


2.86 Cam — In general, a non-circular rotating 
piece in a mechanism. In particular, the device 
which operates the intermittent movement of the 
film in a motion picture projector, camera or printer. 


2.87 Camera Angle — Angle of view taken by the 
motion picture camera. Usually, refers to the 
horizontal angle. 


2.88 Camera Aperture — Diameter of that part of 
the lens used in taking a photograph. 


2.89 Camera Booth — Sound proof booth, 
containing cinematographer and his equipment to 
prevent noise of camera mechanism from reaching 
microphone, 


2.90 Camera Buckle — Jammed film inside the 
camera. 


2.91 Camera Chain — Camera, camera control unit 
and the power supply. 


2.92 Camera Coverage — The area covered by the 
lens of the camera. 


2.93 Camera Crane — Camera platform which can 
be raised. 


2.94 Camera Dolly — Wheel support for carrying 
and moving the camera. 


2.95 Camera Hood — Shield to keep the stray light 
out. 


2.96 Camera Lines — The area covered by the lens 
of the camera. 


2.97 Camera Mount — Any kind of camera 
support other than a tripod. 


2.98 Camera Shifting — The act of rapidly’ 
changing the physical position of the camera lens 


IS 1885 (Part 34) : 2023 


with reference to the fixed subject being 
photographed, or the simulation of the effect of this 
act by other means. 


2.99 Camera Shooting — Photographing the scene 
with a camera. 


2.100 Cam Follower — Component part of film 
feed mechanism cameras. 


2.101 Cam Intermittent movement — Film 
movement intermittent mechanism in which the film 
is transported by means of two rollers one of which 
being provided with a cam. 


2.102 Can — Metal container for film. 


2.103 Cartoon Set — Decor which is drawn in the 
manner as in cartoon. 


2.104 Cascade Printer — Printer in which from one 
negative a number of positives are made in one 
operation. Used, for example, for newsreel films. 


2.105 Cat Walk — Elevated platform containing 
the lights and the men in charge of the lighting. 


2.106 Cell — Single drawing of a cartoon. 


2.107 Cellophane — Plastic substance used for 
carrying the light-sensitive layer. 


2.108 Centre Lens — In a three-lens condenser, the 
middle one of the three lenses. 


2.109 Central Pia Wheel — Driving member of 
double maltese cross. 


2.110 Central Shutter — A shutter placed directly 
in front of the objective, between the lenses or 
directly behind the objective and opening from the 
center. 


2.111 Change Over — In projection, the act of 
changing from one projector to another, preferably 
without interrupting the continuity of projection. 


2.112 Change Over Cue — Marks on the film after 
the motor-cue indicating that tie reel is at the end and 
a new reel should be changed over to. 


2.113 Channel — A complete set of recording 
equipment iron micro phone to film or disk 
recording units inclusive. 


2.114 Cinematograph Camera — Camera for 
taking the images of moving picture films. 


2.115 Cinematography — The art of 
photographically recording motion and reproducing 
it to audiences. 


2.116 Circle-In — To decrease the lens aperture 
gradually. 


2.117 Circle-Out — To increase the lens aperture 
gradually. 


2.118 Clap-Board (Slate) — A card or blackboard 
that contains information pertinent to the scene(s) 
being photographed; generally exposed for several 
frames immediately before each take of a scene. 


2.119 Clap-Stick — A hinged arm attached to the 
clap-board (slate that is photographed at the start of 
each scene to identify it; the sound made by the arm 
when it is brought down on the upper edge of the 
slate is used as a synchronizing guide for picture and 
sound. 


2.120 Clap Mark — The mark obtained on a sound 
film due to the operation clap-stick. 


2.121 Clap Picture — The mark obtained on 
a picture film due to the clap-stick. 


2.122 Claw — Component part of mechanism for 
intermittent movement. 


2.123 Claw Mechanism — Mechanism for giving 
intermittent movement to the film, for example, by 
means of claw pins and pilot pins. 


2.124 Claw Movement — Intermittent movement 
in which the film s moved by two claws or pins 
engaging the perforations. 


2.125 Claw Slipping — Undesired movement in the 
claw mechanism. 


2.126 Claw Supply — The supply of a stretch of 
film by means of the claw movement. 


2.127 Claw Tip — That part of the claw which 
engages with the film perforations. 


2.128 Close Medium Shot — A shot between a 
close-up and a medium shot. 


2.129 Close-Up — Shot of detail of a scene in image 
size. 


2.130 Close-Up View — See close-up, 2.129. 
2.131 Coarse-Grained — A film is coarse-grained 


when the size of the grains is rather large. 


2.132 Coating Head — Part of film coating 
machine, where the emulsion is applied. 


2.133 Collecting Lens — In a three-lens condenser, 
the lens nearest the light source. 


2.134 Colours Fidelity — The degree to which a 
colored picture system is capable of reproducing 
faithfully the colors in an original scene. 


2.135 Colour Film — Film made according to one 
of the processes available in colours. 


2.136 Colour Pilot — Film comprising a succession 
of pairs of negative images taken from all the 
succes8ive scenes in the order in which they occur 
on the original colour negative; a film of this type ii 
used to carry out grading tests and to determine the 
colour balance corrections for printing8 copies. 


2.137 Colour Screen — Colored screen placed 
before electric lamps to change the colour of the 
irradiated object or scene. 


2.138 Commentary — Narrative accompanying 
documentaries. 


2.139 Complicated Shot — A picture that asks for 
special measures in shooting. 


2.140 Composite Shot — Picture consisting of two 
different scenes taken at the same time. 


2.141 Composite Reversal Original — A reversal 
original which has both picture and corresponding 
sound on the same film. 


2.142 Concave Lens — A lens with spherical 
surface thinner at the centre than at the edges. 


2.143 Condenser — An optical device used to 
converge the incident light onto an object. 


2.144 Cone — Conical opaque objects used on 
spotlights for light concentration. 


2.145 Conical Shutter — A shutter of conical form 
in which obstructing blade(s) form a part of the 
conical surface and is placed very close to the 
picture aperture. 


2.146 Contact Printer — Printing machine in 
which the negative is continually in contact with the 
film for making the positive. 


2.147 Contact Printing — See 2.407.2. 
2.148 Contour — See 2.9. 


2.149 Contrast — The ratio of two brightness levels 
in a scene or repro duced picture. 


2.150 Contrast Range — The ratio of the 
brightness of the lightest portion of a picture to that 
of the darkest portion. 


2.151 Converging Lens — In a three-lens 
condenser the lens nearest the objective. 


IS 1885 (Part 34) : 2023 


2.152 Convex Lens — Lens with spherical surface 
thicker at the center than at the edges. 


2.153 Cooling Plate — Component part of a 
cinematograph projector which prevents 
overheating of the mechanism. 


2.154 Core — In mechanical recording the central 
layer or basis support of certain types of laminated 
media. 


2.155 Crane — Apparatus for carrying the camera. 


2.156 Crank — A handle on a camera or projector; 
hardly used any more. 


2.157 Credit Title — The introductory part of the 
film containing the names of the production staff, 
the actors etc and the title. 


2.158 Creeping — Slow irregular up and down 
movement of the picture due to printing from a 
shrunken negative or from uneven shrinking of the 
print itself. 


2.159 Creeping Title — The title of a film which 
appears gradually on the screen from the left to the 
right. 


2.160 Cross-Cutting — Special method of 
obtaining a desired effect by cutting. 


2.161 Cross Wheel (Maltese Cross) — Component 
part of motion picture apparatus for imparting 
intermittent motion to the film, 


2.162 Crowfoot — Camera support preventing 
sliding of the camera. 


2.163 Curved Runner Plate (Film-Skate) — 
Component part of film projector. 


2.164 Cut — In cinematography, suddenly 
changing from one source of vision to another 
(as opposed to fade in or out). 


2.165 Cut-in-Scene — Scene inserted into a 
film and taken apart from it. 


2.166 Cat-Out — Discarded parts of a film by the 
editor or cutter. 


2.167 Cutting and Editing — The final step in 
producing the finished film. 


2.168 Catting Blade — The leading blade of the 
shutter which cuts off the light. 


2.169 Cylindrical Lens — A convex lens the 
contours of which are cylindrical. 


IS 1885 (Part 34) : 2023 


2.170 Dailies — First prints made from original 
picture records of takes’ exposed during a shooting 
scission. 


2.171 Dark Period — The time between two 
exposures during projection. 


2.172 De-Anamorphosing — Term applied in cases 
where anamorphous pictures are restored to the 
normal proportions during printing. 


2.173 Depth of Field — The distance in front of and 
behind the subject in which details remain in 
acceptable focus. 


2.174 Depth of Focus — Range of movement of 
lens that is permissible before unsharpness of object 
to be photographed sets in. 


2.175 Detail Image — Enlarged reproduction of a 
desired part of an image. 


2.176 Detection — A method of inscribing the 
reference marks for preparing lip-sync band 
(see also 2.335). 


2.177 Developer — A chemical solution used to 
bring out the latent image in the exposed areas of the 
light sensitive layer of a plate, film or paper. 


2.178 Developing — Process of chemically treating 
an exposed photographic emulsion to make the 
latent image visible. 


2.179 Developing Hanger — Frame carrying the 
film to be developed. 


2.180 Development Bath — Chemical bath in 
which the latent image is developed. 


2.181 Dialogue — Film comprising only 
the dialogue in the language in which 
post-synchronization has taken place. 


2.182 Dialogue Continuity — Document giving the 
complete text of the dialogue of a film. 


2.183 Diaphragm — In a camera, the iris-like 
device consisting of movable curved blades which 
may be adjusted to control the limiting aperture. 


2.184 Diascope — Projection apparatus for 
diapositives. 


2.185 Diffuser — A precaution used to prevent 
sunlight or artificial light from cantering the lens. 


2.186 Dioptric Lens — Optical apparatus in which 
a number of lenses are placed in a cylindrical 
rotating drum. 


2.187 Director — The production superintendent. 


2.188 Direct Sound Positive — Film carrying the 
photographic wind track, recorded directly as a 
positive. 


2.189 Disc Shutter — Shutter which operates with 
an aperture-obturating disc. It may be single or 
multiple bladed type and it may be placed in float 
or rear. 


2.190 Distance Fog — Occurring with long shot 
exposures. 


2.191 Distortion — Distortion in optical system 
introduced by reason of the fact that the magnifying 
power of the system is not the same in all directions. 


2.192 Diverging lens — A lens which spreads the 
parallel incident light ray. 


2.193 Documentary film — A film on subjects of 
general interest. 


2.194 Doll Bugsy — Wheel support for carrying 
and moving the camera. 


2.195 Dolly In — Decreasing the distance between 
the scene to be photographed and the camera. 


2.196 Dolly Out — Increasing the distance between 
the scene to be photographed and the camera by 
moving the dolly backwards. 


2.197 Dolly Shot — Shooting a moving object and 
keeping at the same distance. 


2.198 Double Claw — Claw with two sets of 
contact points for engaging the perforations. 


2.199 Double Edge — A sound recording on film 
of variable width consisting of two parallel tracks on 
one medium. 


2.200 Downer — A screen to prevent light from 
leaving the projection booth of lamphouse, or in 
general, to prevent the light from the projection lamp 
reaching the film. 


2.201 Drive-In-Theater — An open-air cinema 
theatre where the spectators drive in and sit in their 
cars facing a large screen placed high enough to be 
visible over the cars in front. The space for parking 
each car making on the ground 


2.202 Dram Lens — Optical apparatus in which a 
number of lenses are placed in a cylindrical rotating 
drum. 


2.203 Dram Shutter — Shutter of cylindrical form 
in which the obturating blades form part of the 
cylinder surface. 


2.204 Dabbed Version — Film, the sound section 
of which contains the dialogue dubbed in a language 
other than the language of original recording. 


2.205 Dubbing — All the post-synchronization 
operations in which artist record the dialogue in 
language other than the language of original 
recording, thus supplying the equivalent of the 
original dialogue of a film. 


2.206 Dupe — The copy of a positive or a negative. 
2.207 Dupe Negative — See 2.368.4. 


2.208 Dupe Positive — Positive made from a 
positive. 


2.209 Duping — The art of making a duplicate 
negative or positive, 


2.210 Edge Flare — Unwanted illumination 
occurring at the edge of the picture. 


2.211 Edge Fog — Fog at the edges of the film. 


2.212 Editorial Process — Editorial process is the 
term used to describe the combining, cutting, editing 
and other preparation of material obtained from the 
original material to make the finished motion 
picture. 


2.213 Editorial Script — A document listing the 
successive scenes in an edited film with their 
dialogue and indications of the length and any 
special effects (titles, fades, dissolves, wipes etc). 


2.214 Editorial Synchronism — See 25.13.2. 


2.215 Educational Film — A film for educational 
purposes. 


2.216 Effective Aperture — Diameter of the 
imaginary aperture equal to the real diaphragm 
aperture multiplied by a factor to correct for the 
reduction in apparent size produced by the front 
lens. 


2.217 Effect Lighting — Obtaining special lighting 
effects by means of specially arranged lamps etc. 


2.218 Effect Projector — Special projector used for 
projecting colour and animated scenic effects. 


2.219 Emulsions, Photographic — A photographic 
emulsion consists of dispersion of light-sensitive 
materials in a colloidal medium, usually gelatin, 
carried as a thin-layer on film base. 


NOTE — Photographic materials are usually designated as 
negative or positive types according to their light sensitivity 
(speed) or usage; negative emulsions, in general, being 
more sensitive than positive emulsions. 


IS 1885 (Part 34) : 2023 


2.220 End Title — All the titles at the end of the 
film. 


2.221 Entertainment Film — Film primarily 
intended for entertainment. 


2.222 Episcope — Apparatus for projecting image 
of opaque objects such as postcards, on a screen by 
making use of illumination from the front. 


2.223 Excessive Reverberation — Undesired 
effect arising out of long decay time of sound in an 
enclosure. 


2.224 Exciter Lamp — Lamp used to make 
reproduction of optically recorded sound possible. 


2.225 Exposed Film — Film that has been subject 
to light influences but has not yet been processed. 


2.226 Exposure — Exposing the marginal film to 
the action of light. 


2.227 Exposure Time — The time during which 
each stretch of film is exposed to light. 


2.228 Exposure Timer — Measuring apparatus for 
ascertaining the right exposure time. 


2.229 Fade In — The gradual appearance of a 
picture on the screen. 


2.230 Fade Out — The gradual disappearance of a 
picture on the screen. 


2.231 Fast Motion Effect — By slowing down the 
camera mechanism, the resulting projection will 
show accelerated speed. 


2.232 Feature Film — The essential part of a 
programmer and primarily based on a story or 
theme. 


2.233 Feed Lift — Implement used in film 
processing machines, between the splicing unit and 
the first processing bath. 


2.234 Feed Reel — Reel of film which has not yet 
passed the aperture. 


2.235 Feed Sprocket — The sprocket feeding film 
into the cinematographic apparatus. 


2.236 Fidelity — The exactness with which a 
reproducing system repro duces the original sound 
of picture details. 


2.237 Field of View Limitation — Reduction of the 
field of view by optical means. 


2.238 Field of Vision — The area covered by the 
lens of the camera. 


IS 1885 (Part 34) : 2023 


2.239 Field Pick-Up — The recording of events 
outside the studio by means of cameras, as sports, 
festivities etc. 


2.240 Film — The sensitive material used for 
recording pictures and/or sound. 


2.241 Film Bending — The curvature given to the 
film when in the projector gate. 


2.242 Film Car — Vehicle carrying the filming 
apparatus, for example for newsreel shots. 


2.243 Film Cement — Glueing substance to unite 
two pieces of film. 


2.244 Film Copying Machine — Machine for 
making positive copies from the original negative. 


2.245 Film Drying Drum — Implement used for 
drying processed lengths at film. 


2.246 Film Gate — Movable element which, when 
in operating position, holds the film in proper 
position against the aperture plate. 


2.347 Fila Holder — Implement holding the film 
during developing. 


2.248 Film Length — The length of a film 
expressed in meters. 


2.249 Film Library — A collection of special films 
of scientific and artistic value. 


2.250 Film Loop — A stretch of film formed during 
transport, such as in the projector. 


2.251 Film Margarine — Container for unexposed 
film. 


2.252 Film Processing Apparatus — The complete 
set of apparatus for developing, fixing and drying 
exposed films. 


2.253 Films Rack — Implement holding the film 
during developing. 


2.254 Film Rupture — Breakdown of film 
in camera or projector during transport. 


2.255 Film Speed Indicator Measuring apparatus 
indicating the speed of the film in the 
cinematographic ‘apparatus. 


2.256 Film Splicer — Apparatus for joining the 
ends of two films. 


2.257 Film Threading — The operation of starting 
the film through the projector, camera etc. 


2.258 Film Track — Film guiding component part 
of camera and projector. 


2.259 Fine Grain Master — A fine grain, black and 
white positive film printed from an original negative 
for the purpose of preparing duplicate negatives. 


2.260 Fixing (Fixation) — Film treatment 
subsequent to developing. 


2.261 Flat Picture — Picture that lacks contrast and 
depth. 


2.262 Flicker — The effect which occurs when the 
number of pictures shown on the screen per unit of 
time is not sufficient to ensure complete persistence 
of vision. 


2.263 Flicker Frequency — That value of the 
image frequency at which flicker occurs. 


2.264 Flicker Hitter — Specially designed rotary 
shutter. 


2.265 Flatter — A type of pulsation of pitch in 
reproduced sound. 


2.266 Flutter Effect — Undulatory effect in 
reproduced sound. 


2.267 Focusing — Adjustment of the focus of a 
cinema apparatus to obtain sharp pictures. 


2.268 Focusing Screen — Component part to be 
introduced in the optical axis of the camera for 
accurately locating and focusing scenes. 


2.269 Fog — Darkening of photographic film due to 
its exposure to undesired light or due to poor 
emulsion or to improper development. 


2.270 Fogger — Small incandescent lamp used in 
sound recording to record a fog mark for 
synchronization purposes. 


2.271 Follow-Focus Device — View finder in 
which the focusing mechanism is mechanically 
coupled to the focusing ring on the lens. 


2.272 Follow-Shot — Shooting a moving object and 
keeping at the same distance. 


2.273 Footlight — The row of lights at the front of 
the scene. 


2.274 Four Channel Auditorium Control — 
Volume control to regulate the intensity of the sound 
in the auditorium when reproducing four-channel 
stereophonic films. 


2.275 Four-Channel Stereophonic Film — Picture 
film with four magnetic sound tracks to censure 
stereophonic reproduction. 


2.276 Frame — A single picture on a motion picture 
film. 


2.277 Frame Line — Narrow black border 
separating each picture from the adjacent once. 


2.278 Frame Line Noise — Due to incorrect 
adjustment of the light source for the sound track. 


2.279 Frame Noise — Caused by the film in the 
projector being pulled too far to the right. 


2.280 Framing — Registration of a frame with the 
aperture of a projector during a rest. 


2.281 Fresnel Lenses — Echelon lenses used in 
spot lights, overhead projectors etc. 


2.282 Frilling — Separation of the emulsion from 
the base at the edges. 


2.283 Fringe — Overlapping of colours in colour 
picture. 


2.284 Front Projection — The projection system 
in which the picture is projected upon a 
non-translucent screen. 


2.285 Fort Sinning — Sound reproduction system 
in which the scanning slit is placed between the 
exciter lamp and the film. 


2.286 Front Shutter — Rotary shutter positioned in 
front of the gate aperture or in front of the objective 
lens. 


2.287 Frosts — Frosted glass screen to diffuse light. 


2.288 Gate — Channel in which the film is held fat 
during the exposure or the projection. 


2.289 Gelatin — Colored gelatin screens, placed 
before electric lamps to change the colour of the 
irradiated objects 0: scene. 


2.290 Geometric Distortion — Any aberration 
which causes reproduced picture to be geometrically 
dissimilar to be perspective-plane projection of the 
original scene. 


2.291 Grading Card (Time Card) — A document 
recording the light values (as well as the trichrome 
correction factors) which should be used during 
printing, with the object of equalizing the rendering 
of successive the scenes. 


2.292 Green Film — A film that just has left the 
processing rooms. 


2.293 Halo — Blurring about a bright light part of a 
picture due to various causes. 


IS 1885 (Part 34) : 2023 


2.294 High Angle Shot — A shot taken under a 
certain angle from an elevated spot. 


2.295 High Contrast Image — An image in which 
the contrast between black and white is great and in 
which in terminate tones arc poor. 


2.296 High-Definition Picture — Image with 
highly defined contours. 


2.297 Hot Spot — A bright area of light appearing 
in an image which has been projected by a lens 
system; the spot is usually due to internal reflections 
within the lens. 


2.298 Hunting — Slow regular up and down 
movement, in which the picture regularly and slowly 
drifts up and down the screen. 


2.299 Identification Leader — Length of pictures 
containing 24 frames with real number and picture 
title. 


2.300 Identification Trailer — Consists of 
24 frames containing real number and picture title. 


2.301 Image (Photographic) — Any 
photographically obtained likeness in a processed 
photosensitive material. 


2.301.1 Anamorphic Image — An image which has 
been produced by an optical system having different 
horizontal and vertical magnifications. 


NOTE — Equal horizontal and vertical magnification is 
assumed unless the term anamorphic is applied specially. 


2.301.2 Black and White Image — An image 
produced on a black and white film. 


2.301.3 Colour Image — An image produced on a 
colour film. 


2.301.4 Latent Image — The invisible image 
registered on photographic emulsion due to the 
reaction produced in the emulsion by exposure to 
radiant energy. 


NOTE — This image becomes visible after development. 


2.301.5 Negative Image — A photographic image in 
which the brightness scale is approximately inverted 
with respect to the brightness scale of the original 
subject. In colour negatives the hue scale is usually, 
but not necessarily, complementary to the hue scale 
of the original subject and the brightness scale is 
inverted. 


2.301.6 Picture Image — A photographically 
obtained likeness of any object on photographic 
material. 


2.301.7 Positive Image — A photographic replica in 
which the tones of the gray scale or colour values of 


IS 1885 (Part 34) : 2023 


the originally photographed subject are represented 
in their natural order. 


2.301.383 Sound Image — A photographically 
obtained sound track or sound record. 


2.302 Image Area — The total surface covered by 
the image. 


2.303 Image Contraction — Distortion of the 
reproduced sound track due to under-development 
or under-exposure, 


2.304 Image Growth — Distortion of the 
reproduced sound track due to over-development or 
over-exposure. 


2.305 Incidental Sounds — All sounds as footsteps, 
door bells etc to be incorporated in the final sound 
track. 


2.306 Individual Shot Identification — The mark 
obtained on a sound film due to the clapper boy. 


2.307 Inherent Film Noise — The inherent noise 
present in the film. 


2.308 Insert — Term designating the scenes 
photographed specially to be inserted at the 
designated positions in the translated version. 
Generally used to designate the printed or written 
material. 


2.309 Intermediate Positive (Interpretative) — A 
specially prepared colour print made from an 
original negative for the purpose of making a 
duplicate negative. 


2.310 Intermittent Contact Printer — Printing 
apparatus in which images are transferred from the 
negative on the contacting positive film one by once. 


2.311 Intermittent Mechanism — The mechanism 
feeding the film through the gate. 


2.312 Intermittent Movement — Common type of 
intermittent movement for motion picture cameras. 


2.313 Intermittent Optical Printer — Printing 
apparatus in which images are projected from the 
negative film on the positive film one by one. 


2.314 Intermittent Sprocket — Sprocket behind 
the gate in a projector around which the film is 
drawn taught before a new loop is formed. 


2.315 Internegative — Designation peculiar to 
negative film printed from a reversal original film. 


2.316 Jiggling — Rapid irregular sidewise 
movement caused by grooved guide rollers, 
incorrect or uneven gate tension, misalignment of 


intermittent sprocket shoe, 
intermittent sprocket shaft etc. 


end-play in the 


2.317 Jockey Roller — Roller keeping the film to 
be projected under a certain tension. 


2.318 Jockey Wall — Part of the stage decorations 
that can be easily removed. 


2.319 Jump — Rapid irregular up and down 
movement due to incorrect gate tension, worn 
tension pads etc. 


2.320 Jump in Brightness — The sharp transit from 
black to white in the reproduced picture. 


2.321 Keyhole Mask — A mat placed over the 
camera lens that has an aperture the shape of a 
keyhole. 


2.322 Key Lights — The most important lamps in 
the studio during the shooting. 


2.323 Kicker Light — Light used to illuminate 
shadow regions. 


2.324 Lateral Magnifying Power — The ratio of 
the distance between image point and principal axis 
to that of the congregate object and the axis. 


2.325 Lavender Print — A print on a special film 
for producing a duplicate negative. 


2.326 Protective Leader — Section of unprocessed 
film attached to the beginning and/or end of a reel of 
film. 


2.326.1 Start Leader (Head Leader) — Section of 
film placed at the beginning of each real of film 
material comprising, in addition to the protective 
leader proper, the identification and lacing 
(threading) information relating to projection or 
printing. 


2.327 Lamp House — A housing inopportune a 
light source for projection. 


2.328 Lens Port — Projection room opening for 
letting through the light beam. 


2.329 Lens Screen — A large sheet of metal or 
fabric used to shield moving picture camera lenses 
from light. 


2.330 Lens Hood — A shield, extending beyond the 
lens on the object side, to exclude light from bright 
sources outside the object field without obstructing 
light from the latter. 


2.331 Lens Turret — Part of a camera enabling to 
change the lenses mechanically, hydraulically or 
electrically. 


2.332 Light Screens — Small movable screens used 
with light projectors for controlling the light rays. 


2.333 Light Trap — Implement to prevent light 
falling on the film during the threading of the 
magazine. 


2.334 Lining Up the Camera — Consisting of 
alignment, aspect-ratio adjustment, shading, 
distortion and high peaker test. 


2.335 Lip-Syne Band — Strip comprising the 
oscillogram of the dialogue on which are inscribed 
the corresponding syllables of the test in the 
language in which the film is being dubbed. This test 
is projected in continuous movement with a speed at 
1/8 or 1/12 of the picture film speed, below the 
corresponding picture during the dubbing operation. 


2.336 Locking Claw — A claw which during 
contact with a movie element keeps this in place for 
a short time. 


2.337 Long Shot — Shooting a complete scene 
with human figures, the recording would include the 
feet. 


2.338 Low Angle Shot — A shot taken under 
a certain angle from a low spot. 


2.339 Magnetic Sound Film — A film base having 
film perforations along one or both edges and 
bearing a ferro-magnetic coating either completely 
across the film or in stripes, the coating capable of 
recording and reproducing sound. 


NOTE — Unperforated materials usually are referred to as 
a magnetic tape. 


2.339.1 Full-Coat Magnetic Film — It has the 
magnetic coating compound applied acroas the film 
from edge to edge. 


2.339.2 Full-Coat Between Perforations Magnetic 
Film — It has the magnetic coating compound 
across the film from perforation to perforation. 


2.339.3 Magnetic Master — It is a final edited or 
re-recorded magmatic sound record used for transfer 
to a magnetic release print or for transfer to a 
photographic sound negative to be used for 
manufacturing prints with photographic sound 
tracks. 


2.339.4 Magnetic Original — It is the original or 
first sound record on a magnetic film. 


2.339.5 Magnetic Transfer — A magnetic sound 
record obtained by electrical re-recording of a 
magnetic original onto another mange tic film. 


2.340 Magnetic Striping — This is a process by 
which a magnetic coating compound is applied in 
the form of single or multiple stripes, having specific 


IS 1885 (Part 34) : 2023 


widths and placements, to either surface of a film 
base which may or may not have a photographic 
emulsion. 


2.341 Main and Credit Title — All the titles at the 
beginning of a film. 


2.342 Maltese-Cross — See 2.161 


2.343 Married Print — Processed film containing 
picture and sound tracks in their correct relationship. 


2.344 Mask — Device to limit the effective area of 
the picture. 


2.345 Mask Shot — A shot in which a mask is used 
to obtain desired effects. 


2.346 Master Control — Switching point and 
central place for the grouping of amplifiers etc. 


2.347 Master Print — The print from which the 
duplicate negative is painted. 


2.348 Master Shot — A shot taken to reproduce the 
whole scene. 


2.349 Master Sound Track — Complete sound 
track to be married to the picture film. 


2.350 Matte Rolls — film rolls used as light 
modulators in printing machines for obtaining 
transitional effects. 


2.351 Medium Close-Up — A shot between a 
close-up and a medium shot. 


2.352 Medium Long Shot — A shot between a long 
shot and a medium shot. 


2.353 Medium Shot — Shot between close-up and 
long shot. With human figures, it does not generally 
include feet, 


2.354 Meridional Focal Line — The focal line at 
right angles to the plane passing through the 
principal axis of the lens and the axis of the beam of 
light. 


2.355 Milled Edge — Notches made in the edges of 
negative films to control the copying light intensity. 


2.356 Mirror — The reflecting means behind the 
arc-lamp or lamphouse. 


2.357 Misframing — The picture not correctly 
framed; said also when a splice is wrongly made. 


2.358 Mixing — The process by which the sound 
tracks of the dialogue, sound effects and music, 
separately recorded, are clerically mixed at their 
respective levels in order to constitute the final 
sound score of the film. 


IS 1885 (Part 34) : 2023 


2.359 Motion Picture Equipment — A complete 
set of sound and image reproducing apparatus, 
auxiliary apparatus etc tor motion picture theatres. 


2.360 Motion Picture Film — A thin flexible 
ribbon of transparent plastic having perforations and 
bearing one or more sensitized layers capable of 
producing photographic images. 

NOTE — The term ‘Film’ may be applied to unexposed 


film, to exposed but unprocessed film, and to exposed and 
processed film. 


2.361 Motion Picture Projector Head — The 
apparatus for projecting recorded images and is a 
part of a motion picture equipment. 


2.362 Motion Picture Projector — A composite 
apparatus required for screening motion pictures and 
their accompanying sound tracks. 


2.363 Motor Cue — Circular opaque marks with 
transparent outline printed from the negative which 
has had four consecutive frames punched with a die 
2.39 mm in diameter. It indicates that the end is near 
and the motor should be started for the changeover 
(see also 2.111 and 2.112). 


2.364 Montage — The juxtaposition or partial 
superposition of a number of individual scenes to 
form a complete picture. 


2.365 Music and Effects Track (Museffex) — 
Film with a magnetic or photographic sound record 
comprising the mixture of music and sound effects 
(without dialogue) this section is intended to be 
mixed with the dialogue prepared at the time of 
dubbing in order to complete the sound section of 
the dubbed version of the film. 


2.366 Music and Vocals — Film comprising a 
magnetic or photographic sound record of vocals 
and music to be mixed with the other parts of the 
sound. 


2.367 Narrow Gauged Film — Any film with a 
width smaller than 32 mm. 


2.368 Negative — Film (black and white or colour) 
comprising, after processing, pictures in which the 
brightness scale is inverse to the scene brightness; 
this may also refer to, a sound track. 


2.368.1 Background Plate Negative — A picture 
negative which is used for printing background 
plates. 


2.368.2 Combined Duplicate Negative — A 
duplicate negative on which have been printed the 
picture and corresponding sound track, with the 
standard picture/sound relationship for release 
prints. 


12 


2.368.3 Combined Negative — Negative film con 
training pictures and sound recordings. 


2.368.4 Duplicable Negative — Film with negative 
images made from intermediate positives on a 
special film material by one or more successive 
printing stages. 


2.368.5 Foreign Picture Release Negative — A 
picture release negative prepared specifically for 
printing forcing version release prints. 


NOTE — It is almost invariably a duplicate negative. 


2.368.6 Original Picture Negative — The negative 
film that was exposed in a camera and processed to 
produce a negative image of the original subject. 


2.368.7 Picture Negative — Film comprising 
negative picture images made as a result of exposure 
and cutting. It is intended for making positive prints 
and duplication materials. 


2.368.8 Picture Duplicate (Dupe) Negative — A 
picture negative made from black and white, colour 
or separation master positive films. 

NOTE — It may be used for making additional prints or it 


may be cut and edited to form a part of the picture release 
negative. 


2.368.9 Picture Library Negative — A picture 
negative that is usually held in a film library for use 
in reproducing scenes which would otherwise have 
to be made as original material for each production. 


2.368.10 Picture Release Negative — A cut and 
edited picture negative used for printing the picture 
portion of release prints. 
NOTE — It may consist of intercut original picture 
negative, picture dupe negatives, etc, depending upon the 
film-processing technique to be employed in making release 
print. 


2.368.11 Release Negative — A release negative is 
a complete negative prepared specifically for 
printing release prints. 
NOTE — A release negative may consist of separate picture 
and sound negative and may be either projection or editorial 


synchronism, depending upon the film-processing 
technique to be employed in making release prints. 


2.368.12 Titles Negative — Film comprising only 
negative images of titles. 


2.369 Negative Cutting — Process by which the 
original and other negative elements are cut and 
assembled to constitute the final edited version of a 
film. 


2.370 Negative Distortion — Distortion of the 
picture, in which the sides bulge like a pincushion. 


2.371 Negative Raw Stock — Black and white or 
colour film intended for the recording of picture or 
sound in negative form. 


2.372 Negative Raw Stock with Positive 
Perforations — Negative film having perforations 
identical to those of the standard positive film. 


2.373 News Reel — Film showing current events 
from all parts of the world. 


2.374 Nitrate Film — Film on a cellulose nitrate 
base. 


2.375 One to One — Term applied to cases where 
the images are reproduced in the same size. 


2.376 Observation Hole — Opening or window in 
the wall of the projection room for observing the 
projected picture. 


2.377 Optical Axis — The straight line through the 
centers of the light source, lenses etc. 


2.378 Optical Compensation — Means to 
compensate the picture displacement in continuous 
systems. 


2.379 Optical Printing — Operation of printing by 
exposure ofraw stock via an optical system from the 
film to be printed. 


2.380 Optical Reduction Printing Equipment — 
Equipment for carrying out the reduction printing 
process. 


2.381 Optical Scratch — Due to dirt or mechanical 
imperfection in the slit of the projector. 


2.382 Optical Sound Reorder — Equipment 
incorporating means for producing a modulated 
light beam and means for moving a light-sensitive 
medium relative to the beam for recording signals 
derived from sound signals. 


2.383 Optical Sound Reproducer — A 
combination of light source, optical system, 
photoelectric cell, or other light-sensitive device 
and a mechanism for moving a medium carrying an 
optical sound record (usually film), by means of 
which the recorded variations may be converted into 
electric signals of approximately like form. 


2.384 Optical View Finder — View finder which 
works optically. 


2.385 Overdeveloped — Said of a film when the 
result of the developing’ process is that the picture 
is short of white. 


2.386 Over-Exposure — Resulting in complete loss 
of gradation in the developed picture. 


IS 1885 (Part 34) : 2023 


2.387 Overhead Scoop — A twin-arc light 
suspended over the set. 


2.388 Over-Lighting — The lighting of the scene 
by means of light lources over it. 


2.389 Pan Master rom Colour — Black and white 
positive printed on panchromatic emulsion from a 
reversal original film. 


2.390 Pan — The movement of the camera in a 
horizontal plane from one point of the set to another, 


NOTE — Camera movement in a vertical plane is referred 
to as ‘tilt’. 


2.391 Perfect Shot — A perfect photographic take. 


2.392 Perforated Screen — Screen with a large 
number of small openings to allow the sound from 
the loudspeaker to pass into the auditorium. 


2.393 Perforation (Film) — Holes punched in the 
film to engage the teeth of the sprockets. 


2.394 Persistence of Vision — Sensation of light, 
as interpreted by the brain persists for a brief interval 
after the actual light stimulus is removed; successive 
images, if they follow one another sufficiently 
rapidly, produce aa continuous impression. Use is 
made of this in the motion picture presentation. 


2.395 Pitch (Film Perforation) — The distance 
between the Centre of two perorations of a film. 


2.396 Positive — Film, black and white or colour, 
which after printing and processing, contains images 
having rendition of light and shade as in the original 
subject; this may also refer to a sound track. 


2.397 Positive Raw Stock — Black and white or 
colour raw stock intended for printing from negative 
picture and/or sound elements. 


2.398 Positive Raw Stock with Negative 
Perforations — Positive black and white or colour 
having perforations identical to those of negative 
film. Usually used in special effects photography. 


2.399 Positive Release Printer — Photographic 
processing machine producing the married print. 


2.400 Postsynchronising — The series of 
operations recording in synchronism for the pictures 
with dialogue, sound effects and music which 
produce the sound track. 


2.401 Photographic Sound — A sound record in 
the form of a photographic image. 


2.402 Prescoring — Said when sound is recorded 
before a picture is made. 


IS 1885 (Part 34) : 2023 


2.403 Pressure Gate — Component part of film 
guiding mechanism. 


2.404 Pressure Guide — Component part of film 
projector. 


2.405 Pressure Pad — Felt pads mounted on brass- 
spring arms which hold the film or tape in close 
contact with the head. 


2.406 Print — The developed film after being 
printed from the negative. 


2.406.1 Check Print — Corrected or not fully 
corrected silent or sound positive print made to 
check the physical or photographic condition of the 
negative printing elements and, where necessary, the 
synchronism. 


2.406.2 Composite Print — A positive film having 
both picture and corresponding sound on the same 
him, which may be in editorial or projection 
synchronism. 


2.406.3 Composite Daily Print — A composite daily 
print is made from an original composite negative or 
original sound and picture negatives, and is used for 
checking photography, sound quality, action etc. 
It is in projection synchronism. 


2.406.4 Composite Master Positive — A composite 
print usually made for the purpose of producing 
composite or picture and sound duplicate negatives 
which would be used for printing release prints. 


NOTE — It is usually made on duplicating positive film and 
may be in either editorial or projection synchronism. 


2.406.5 Dubbing Print — Positive print made from 
the cut negative or dupe negative and intended for 
cutting up into elementary scenes mounted in loops 
for dubbing operations. 


2.406.6 Final Trial Composite — A composite print, 
approved for release, in which all corrections found 
necessary in previous trial composite prints have 
been incorporated. 

NOTE — The final trial composite may be any one of the 


various trial composite prints, depending upon the type and 
extent of correctional required. 


2.406.7 First Trial Composite Print — The first 
composite print made from the picture and sound— 
release negatives for the purpose of checking and 
correcting picture and sound quality, negative 
cutting and assembly, etc. It is in projection 
synchronism. 


2.406.8 Foreign Version Trial Composite Prints — 
These are similar to trial composite prints made 
during release, except that they are made for 
checking the release of the particular language 
version involved. 


14 


2.406.9 Panchromatic Master Position, 35 mm — It 
is a black and white print made on a panchromatic 
film from a colour negative for the purposes of 
making a black and white duplicate negative. 


2.406.10 Picture Print — A picture print is a 
processed film that possesses a positive picture 
image of the subject or film image to which it was 
exposed. 


2.406.11 Picture Daily Print — The first picture 
print made from the original picture negative for use 
in checking photographic quality, camera technique 
actions etc. 


2.406.12 Picture Library Print — A picture print 
made from a picture library negative. 


2.405.13 Picture Master Positive — A print usually 
made on a special film for the purpose of producing 
picture duplicate negatives. 


2.406.14 Picture Work Print — A positive print 
which usually consists of intercut picture daily 
prints, picture library prints, prints of dissolves, 
montages, titles etc and has synchronism constantly 
maintained with the corresponding sound work 
print. 


2.406.15 Reduction Reversal Print, 16 mm — A 
reversal print made on 16 mm reversal film from a 
35 mm positive by reduction printing and 
development by the reversal process. 


2.406.16 Reference Print — Black and white or 
colour print made in optimum reference conditions, 
and with which series—produced release prints 
must conform. 


2.406.17 Release Print — See 2.435. 


2.406.18 Reversal Print — Film having a positive 
image obtained by printing from positive material. 


2.406.19 Reversal Master Print, 16 mm — A 16mm 
reversal print made specifically for use in producing 
other prints. 


NOTE — It is sometimes referred to as a rot generation 
duplicate, print am it then being referred to as record 
generation duplicates. 


2.406.20 Second, Third etc, Trial Composites Print 
— It is similar to the first trial composite print, but 
has successive corrections incorporated as a result 
of viewing the previous trial composite prints. 


2.406.21 Television Print — Positive print with or 
without a sound record made especially for 
transmission by telecine equipment. 


2.407 Printing — Printing is the operation of 
exposing raw stock by using the processed image of 
another film as the light modulator. 


2.407.1 A and B Printing — This is a method of 
making composite images, such as fades, dissolves 
or effects, in a release printer without requiring a 
duplicating process. 
NOTE — The name comes from the fact that the films are 
edited into two separates rolls called A and B rolls. The 
sequences of pictures originally in one roll are in 
synchronization with opaque leader in the other roll, when 
these two are printed in a separate operation on to a single 
roll of raw stock, an opportunity is afforded for the 


introduction of effects and for eliminating visible splices on 
the screen. 


2.407.2 Contact Printing — Operation of printing 
by exposure of raw stock in direct contact with the 
film to be printed. 


2.407.2.1 Continuous contact printing — A method 
of contact printing by which the light modulating 
film and the raw stock move at the same constant 
speed past the printing aperture. 


2.407.2.2 Step contact printing — A method of 
contact printing an which the film being copied and 
the raw stock are advanced intermittently frame-by- 
frame, being exposed to the printer light only when 
stationary. 


2.407.2.3 Projection printing (optical printing) — 
See 2.379 


2.408 Printing Tape — A perforated strip or tape 
(usually paper) which provides information 
concerning the necessary changes of the printing 
light conditions. 


2.409 Printer Factor — The difference in density 
produced on the positive copies by the various 
printers. 


2.410 Printer Starmark — Reference marks on the 
picture and sound track leader for effecting proper 
lacing (threading) of films in printing machines so 
as to achieve synchronization between picture and 
sound. 


2.411 Print Grader — Operator in the laboratory 
who tries to obtain the best result from the negative 
supplied for making copies. 


2.412 Priesting Lose — Loss in sound quality due 
to the copying processes used. 


2.413 Processing — This is a generic term applied 
to the total operation necessary to produce a 
permanent visible image on exposed film. 


2.414 Production — A general term used to 
describe the processes involved in making all the 


15 


IS 1885 (Part 34) : 2023 


original material that is the basis for the finished 
motion picture. 


2.415 Projection Distance — The distance between 
the projecting lens and the center of the projected 
picture. 


2.416 Projection Room — A room or enclosure 
from which motion pictures are projected. 


2.417 Projection Screen — The surface on which 
pictures are projected. 


2.417.1 Matte While Screen — Projection screen 


with a magnesium oxide surface having 
non-specular finish. 
2.417.2 Lenticular Screen — Projection screen 


covered with small bead shaped particles or heavily 
embossed for maximum diffusion, giving high 
reflectance but relatively small viewing angle. 


NOTE — They may be pearl or aluminum coated. 


2.418 Projector Efficiency — The transmitting 
efficiency of an electro acoustic transducer is the 
ratio of the total acoustic power output to the electric 
power input. In computing the electric power input, 
it is customary to omit any electric power supplied 
for polarization or bias. 


2.419 Projector Head — See 2.361. 


2.420 35 mm Protection Master Positive — A 
positive film made from the final cut and edited 
black and white or colour release negative. In case 
of damage to the release negative, a duplicity 
‘negative could be made from this protection master 
positive in the case of colour, this protection master 
positive will be the colour master positive. 


2.421 Protective Track — Designation of the 
transfer on magnetic film of either the dialogue track 
or the music and effects track, with a view to 
keeping the original track intact. 


2.422 Protective Trailer — Strip of film at end of 
reel identical to protective head leader. 


2.423 Publicity Stills — Set of photograph prints of 
scans from a film which are intended for publicity 
purposes when the latter is released to cinemas. 


2.424 Push-Pull Track — Sound track with two 
recordings so arrange that the modulation in one is 
exactly 180° out of phase with that in the other. 


2.425 Rain Effect — Fault in the reproduced picture 
due to a wrong relation between the maltese cross 
and the position of the shutter blade. 


2.426 Raw Stock Film — A film which has not 
been exposed or processed. 


IS 1885 (Part 34) : 2023 


2.427 Real Image — Image through which the light 
rays actually pass, such as the image formed by a 
lens on the ground glass or photographic film of a 
camera (image is always inverted). 


2.428 Rear Projection — The picture projected on 
a translucent screen from behind and in which 
projected picture can be viewed by the spectator 
sitting in front of the screen. 


2.429 Rear Scanning — Sound reproducing system 
in which the film is placed between the exciter lamp 
and the scanning slit. 


2.430 Reduction Printing — Optical printing 
where the picture or sound record is printed on a film 
with a smaller image size than that of the film to be 
printed. 


2.431 Reduction Printing Process — Process for 
converting standard film pictures to narrow gauge 
(substandard) film pictures. 


2.432 Reel and Tray Processing Machine — 
Processing machine using reels and trays for film 
lengths up to 60 m. 


2.433 Reflecting Screen — Screen used to 
compensate shadow parts with diffused light. 


2.434 Relative Aperture — The ratio d : f, in which, 
d is the diameter of the aperture and the effective 
focal length of the lens. 


2.435 Release Print — Positive print made from the 
original negative or the duplicate negative for 
distribution purposes; the sound is in the form of a 
photographic sound track or stripped magnetic track 
or both (MAGOP). 


2.435.1 Anamorphic Release Print — A release 
print in which the picture image is compressed 
laterally, requiring a de-anamorphosing lens on the 
projector to cause objects in the projected picture to 
have correct proportions, 


2.435.2 Composite Release Print — A print having 
both picture and sound records in projection 
synchronism on the same film. 


NOTE — The sound record may be photographic or 
magnetic or both. 


2.435.3 Domestic Release Print — A release print 
intended for distribution within the country where 
the print was manufactured and having dialogue in 
the language of that country. It may be a composite 
print or may have magnetic sound track or tracks od 
a separate film. 


2.435.4 Foreign Version Release Print — A 
composite print in projection synchronism with 


16 


dialogue made specifically for the particular 
language involved. 


NOTE — Sometimes superimposed titles in a different 
language are used on the print. A superimposed title 
consists of printed words (usually transparent) overlaying 
the picture magic. 


2.435.5 Magoptical Release Print — A composite 
release print which has both magnetic and 
photographic (optical) sound tracks. 


2.435.6 Wide-Screen Release Print — A print which 
has no anamorphosis but, when projected, produces 
a screen image having an aspect ratio greater than 
1.33 to 1. 


NOTE — Some prints are made from negative exposed in a 
camera aperture having an aspect ratio of 1.33 to 1, but 
which have been composed for projection to yield a 
projected picture having an aspect ratio greater than 1.33 
to 1. A wide—screen print may also be obtained from an 
anamorphic negative by de-anamorphosing in the print 
process, 


2.436 Remote Recording — The recording of 
events outside the studio by means of camera, as 
sports, royal festivities etc. 


2.437 Re-Recording — The electrical process of 
transferring sound records from one or more films, 
magnetic tapes or discs to other films, tapes or discs. 


2.438 Resolving Power — The quality of a lens or 
of a light-sensitive emulsion, indicating in how far 
closely adjoining clements of an object can be 
reproduced separately. 


2.439 Reverse Action — Projection of a film from 
end to start. 


2.440 Reversal Film — A reversal film is one 
which, after an exposure, is processed by a first 
development, a bleach and a redevelopment to 
reduce a positive image. Exposure is made by 
printing from a negative, a negative image is 
produced by the reversal process. 


2.441 Reversal Original Film — A reversal 
original is the film that is originally exposed in a 
camera or recorder and is processed by reversal to 
produce a positive image. 


NOTE — This positive image obtained by the reversal 
proceed is not the same as pint from a negative inasmuch a 
right and lilt are transposed; when viewed by pro section on 
an opaque screen, the emulsion side of the print, from a 
negative must face the light source and the emulsion vide of 
a reversal original must face the lens in order for the screen 
image to have the same lateral orientation as the original 
scene. 


2.442 Reversal Positive — Film resulting from the 
printing of a reversal original and carrying images 
or an optical sound track or both. 


2.443 Reversal Raw Stock — Film suitable for 
reversal processing which makes it possible to 
obtain directly, after shooting or printing, black and 
white or colour images corresponding to the 
originals. 


2.444 Rewinding — The process of reversing the 
winding of a film. 


2.445 Roiling — Tilting the camera on its horizontal 
axis sideways. 


2.446 Rolling Title — A title, the lines of which 
traverse the picture. 


2.447 Rotating Shutter — A shutter consisting of a 
fat circular disk which rotates around its center. A 
hole is made in the disk for the exposure. 


2.448 Runner Plate — Film guiding component 
part of camera and projector. 


2.449 Rush Print — Print of a film to be presented 
to the producer etc, the same day it is taken. 


2.450 Safety Film — Fire-resistant cinema film. 


2.451 Safety Fire-Trap — Means to localize the 
burning of a film in the projector. 


2.452 Sagittal Focal Line — The focal lines 
occurring in astigmatism lying in the plane passing 
through the principal axis of the lens and the axis of 
the beam of light. 


2.453 Scanning Beam — A beam of light thrown 
on the film used in the process of recording and 
reproduction. 


2.454 Seaming Gate — Component part of sound 
film reproduction apparatus containing the scanning 
slit. 


2.455 Scamming Slit — Slit in scanning gate to let 
through light rays from the exciter lamp for sound 
reproduction from an optical track. 


2.456 Scenario — The manuscript containing all 
details about the shots to be taken. 


2.457 Scenery — The art of presenting the scenery 
in an artistic and realistic way. 


2.458 Scratching — Damage to the film surface. 


2.459 Serene Brightness — The attribute of the 
visual appearance by which the screen seems to emit 
more or less light. 


2.460 Screen Tower — Building construction in 
drive-in theatre carrying the screen or screens, 
preferably at a certain viewing angle. 


IS 1885 (Part 34) : 2023 


2.461 S-Distortion — Horizontal lines tending to 
twist up or down as the camera moves across. 


2.462 Sensitive Layer — The light sensitive layer 
on photographic material. 


2.463 Sensitometer — Apparatus for measuring the 
sensitivity of film's emulsion. 


2.464 Sensitometry — The measurement of the 
light-response characteristics of photographic film 
under specified conditions of exposure and 
development. 


2.465 Separate Effects Track — Film comprising 
a magnetic or photographic record of only the sound 
effects to be mixed with the other parts of the sound. 


2.466 Separate Music Track — Film comprising a 
magnetic or photographic sound record of the 
musical part to be mixed with the other parts of the 
sound. 


2.467 Separate Music and Effects Track — Film 
with two or more magnetic sound records 
comprising the separate music and effects tracks of 
a sound score. 


2.468 Separation — Printing operation carried out, 
starting from a colour original, on a black and white 
film, with a suitable filter. 


2.469 Separation Master — Black and white film 
obtained in the course of separation printing. 


2.470 Separation Positive Film, 35 mm — A 
35 mm separation positive is a black and white film 
with a positive image of the red, green or blue image 
component of a colour negative. It is usually made 
by printing through suitable filters from a colour 
negative onto a panchromatic black and white film. 


2.471 Shooting Tricks — Special measures taken 
mostly in a special room for making pictures by 
means of, for example, a trick table, 


2.472 Shutter — A device usually automatic to 
admit and cut off light for a predetermined interval 
of time to enable photographic exposures to be 
made. 


2.473 Shutter Aperture — The actual diameter of 
the lens surface used during taking photographs. 


2.474 Shutter Axis — The axis of the rotating 
shutter. 


2.475 Shutter Frequency — Usually kept at 48 
interruptions per second. 


2.476 Silent Film — Film without accompanying 
recorded sound. 


IS 1885 (Part 34) : 2023 


2.477 Silent Positive — Film printed from a 
negative with the frame format in use before the 
introduction of sound. 


2.478 Sky Backing — A backing with sky details, 
often used in close-ups. 


2.479 Slide Projector — A still projector used in 
cinema auditorium. 


2.480 Slow Motion Effect — The resulting 
projection at normal speed showing a slow motion 
of the performers obtained by accelerating the 
camera mechanism. 


2.481 Sound Booth — Sound-proof room for 
containing the sound camera. 


2.482 Sound Effects — Artificially produced 
accompanying sound. 


2.483 Sound Fading Device — Potentiometer used 
to control volume of sound in reproduction, also that 
used to control intensity of the printer lights. 


2.484 Sound Film — Picture film with 
accompanying sound optically or otherwise 
recorded on the same or a separate medium. 


2.485 Sound Print — Any positive obtained by 
printing from a sound negative, or direct positive 
recording, or by the reversal process, from another 
sound positive. A sound print provides a reasonably 
faithful reproduction of the original sound through 
the conventional scanning system. 


2.485.1 Music Print — A sound print made from 
a music negative. 


2.485.2 Re-recorded Print — A sound print from a 
re-recorded sound-track negative. 


2.485.3 R-recording Print — A sound print prepared 
specifically for use in re-recording to produce a 
re-recorded negative. 


2.485.4 Sound Check Print — A sound print made 
from the sound release negative for the purpose of 
checking negative cutting, printing lights, sound 
quality etc. 


2.485.5 Sound Daily Print — The first sound print 
made from the original sound negative for checking 
sound quality, technique, etc. 


2.485.6 Sound-Effects Pint — A sound print made 
from a sound-effects negative, or from another 
sound-effects print by reversal processing. 


2.485.7 Sound Master Positive — A sound print on 
special film stock that is usually made from a sound 
release negative for the purpose of producing 


duplicate negatives of the sound record for release 
printing. 


2.485.8 Sound Work Print — A sound print that 
usually consists of intercut sound daily prints, but 
may also include other sound tracks of sound effects 
or music, or both, on the same or separate films, with 
synchronism constantly maintained with the 
corresponding picture work print. 


2.486 Sound Gate — Gate through which the sound 
record on the film is pulled past the reproducing 
light beam. 


2.487 Sound Head (Sound Reproducer) — That 
part of the motion picture equipment that contains 
the optical elements of the sound reproducing 
equipment. 


2.488 Sound Negative — Film comprising negative 
images of a photographic sound record. It is 
intended for making positive prints. 


2.488.1 Music Negative — A sound negative upon 
which music has been recorded. It is usually an 
original sound negative but may be a library 
negative. 


2.488.2 Original Sound Negative — The sound 
negative that is exposed in a film recorder and, after 
processing, produces a negative sound image on the 
film. 


2.488.3 Re-recorded Negative — A sound negative 
which is exposed by rerecording and, when 
processed, produces a negative sound track image. 


2.488.4 Sound Cut Negative — A sound negative 
that is composed of sections of original sound 
negatives spliced in sequence. 


2.488.5 Sound-Effects Negative— A sound negative 
upon which sound effects have been recorded. It is 
ordinarily held, in library stock. 


2.488.6 Sound Release Negative — A photographic 
sound negative in the form required for the final 
printing operation onto the release print raw stock. 


2.489 Sound Negative Raw Stock — A negative 
raw stock, the emulsion of which is specially 
designed for sound recording. 


2.490 Sound Positive — A film carrying only a 
positive photographic sound track. 


2.491 Sound Speed — Speed at which sound 
pictures are fed through the cinema apparatus 
equivalent to 24 frames per second. 


2.492 Sound Track — A narrow band, usually 
along the margin of a sound film, which carries the 


sound record. In some cases, a plurality of such 
bands may be used. 


2.493 Spherical Aberration — The aberration that 
occurs when, with increasing aperture angle, the 
incident rays are focused on different points on the 
axis. 


2.494 Splicing — Joining together different pieces 
of processed films. 


2.495 Splicing Cement — Glueing substance to 
unite two pieces of film. 


2.496 Split Reel — A reel of film of two or more 
parts. 


2.497 Spot Light — A light source capable of 
projecting a focused beam of light to a specific part 
of the set or stage 


2.498 Sprocket — The toothed roller engaging the 
perorations of the film. 


2.499 Sprocket Hum (Noise) — The 96 Hz note 
due to the film running out of alignment with the 
scanning beam. 


2.500 Squeegee — Implement for removing all the 
free surface moisture from the film before drying. 


2.501 Star Wheel — See 2.161. 


2.502 Steadiness — The absence of undesirable 
movement of the image as a whole. 


2.503 Stereophonic Effect — Effect obtained by 
hearing sound with two cars. 


2.504 Stereophonic Sound System — A sound 
system in which a plurality of microphones, 
transmission channels and loudspeakers are 
arranged so as to provide a sensation of spatial 
distribution of the sound sources to the listener of 
the reproduction. 


2.505 Still — Photographic or other stationary 
illustrative material which may be used in a studio. 


2.506 Still Projection — Projection of a single 
image for chucking purposes etc. 


2.507 Subtitle Cue Sheet — Document listing the 
texts of successive subtitles with an indication of the 
start and finish of each subtitle, 


2.508 Subtitles — Texts inscribed within the picture 
area of a print either by photographic printing or by 
engraving and generally used to give an abbreviated 
translation of the dialogic in another language. 


2.509 Superimposing — The superimposing of two 
or more images. 


IS 1885 (Part 34) : 2023 


2.510 Supply Reel — The spool containing the film 
going to be played and to be inserted in the feeding 
mechanism. 


2.511 Sync Beep (Sound Pulse) — A sound pulse 
of short duration recorded on the photographic or 
magnetic track defining synchronism with that 
picture frame which shows the close of the clapper 
or the light of a lamp. 


2.512 Synchronization Mark — Marks on the 
picture film and its related sound film to provide 
after printing data for relating the picture to the 
corresponding sound. 


2.513 Synchronism — Synchronism is the relation 
between the picture and sound with respect either to 
the physical location on the film or films or to the 
time at which corresponding picture and sound are 
seen and heard. 


2.513.1 Camera Synchronism — Camera 
synchronism is the relation between picture and 
sound track in a composite camera original. 


2.513.2 Editorial Synchronism — Editorial 
synchronism is the relationship between the picture 
and sound film during the editorial process. 


2.513.3 Projection Synchronism — Projection 
synchronism is the time relation between picture and
